text: Opening, 30 seconds. Introduce the team and problem WO-012. A QRNG uses quantum measurements as a randomness source. Q-Sentinel examines its digitized output and helps engineers investigate changes. Our prototype uses files and classical simulated streams. Team 55, Gladiators. Members: Ashin R, Akhash A, Anushek RK, Astlin Dijo D, Aravind R. Source: user-supplied six-slide outline and q-sentinel/README.md.

text: About 45 seconds. Noise, bit bias, dependence, detector operating conditions, acquisition timing and post-processing can affect observed output. These are possible contributors, not diagnoses from bits alone. A pass/fail statistical summary is useful but does not itself explain the timeline. Avoid claiming all existing tools lack monitoring. Early detection is an objective evaluated in simulations, not a guarantee for every fault. Source: user outline, q-sentinel/README.md.

text: About 55 seconds. Entropy fingerprinting combines normalized anomalies and raw metrics such as marginal Shannon/min entropy, bias, correlation, runs and spectral characteristics. Rule-based signatures describe behavior consistent with bias, correlation, periodicity, bursts or repetition. They do not prove hardware causes. The Failure Lab supports controlled faults. Forecasts are conditional projections and may be unavailable. The added value is connecting monitoring, first-detection evidence and engineering follow-up. Sources: user outline; q-sentinel/README.md.

text: About 65 seconds. Inputs currently include TXT, CSV and binary files plus the simulator. CUSUM accumulates deviations from a frozen baseline, with calibration and persistence rules. An initial 30-window baseline is unverified unless supplied reference data is available. Six NIST families: Frequency, Block Frequency, Runs, Longest Run, DFT and Cumulative Sums forward/backward. Marginal entropy does not capture all sequence predictability. NIST passes do not certify quantum origin or security. SQLite stores history, and ReportLab produces PDF reports. Serial, TCP/WebSocket and MQTT adapters remain future integration points. Sources: q-sentinel/README.md; NIST SP 800-22 Rev.1a https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/22/r1/upd1/final.

text: About 60 seconds. The MVP runs on a Windows laptop using mature Python libraries. The digital twin is an engineering-level classical simulation, not quantum physics simulation. Evaluation used five seeds and 75 fault scenarios; 71 were detected and 4 missed. There were 2 false alert events over 350 healthy monitoring windows. Do not describe 71/75 as overall accuracy. Early-warning comparison had 16 earlier detections, 41 simultaneous, 3 later and 15 without jointly available times. Do not claim every fault is found before NIST. A real-data lab pilot is required. AWS EC2, Linux and Docker are proposed deployment targets, not verified current deployments. Actual costs depend on resources and usage. Sources: q-sentinel/output/evaluation-summary.json; q-sentinel/VALIDATION.md; user outline.

text: Closing, about 45 seconds. Potential application areas include QRNG development for cryptographic key generation, secure communication, authentication, quantum networks and research. These are intended use areas, not current customers or certified production deployments. First detection is not necessarily the true physical onset. Trend projections require sufficient consistent evidence and are conditional. The next milestone is validation against real QRNG recordings and hardware measurements. End with: Q-Sentinel helps engineers understand when randomness changes, what evidence supports the warning, and what to investigate next. Offer the Failure Lab demo, using actual displayed values rather than promising an alert order. Sources: user outline; q-sentinel/README.md.
